anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > The cathode-ray oscilloscope graticule: "The screen is a calibrated grid where the vertical axis shows potential difference and the horizontal axis shows elapsed time."
purpose: Define the coordinate system of a cathode-ray oscilloscope screen graticule, contrasting the vertical potential difference scale (y-gain) with the horizontal linear time sweep (time-base).
what_to_show: Rectangular graticule grid of 8 major horizontal divisions by 6 major vertical divisions. Major division lines are solid lines at 1.0 cm intervals; each major division contains 5 subdivisions at 0.2 cm intervals marked along the central axes. A dashed horizontal centre line marks y = 0. A vertical dimension bracket at the left is labelled 'Vertical displacement = potential difference (scaled by y-gain in V/div)'. A horizontal dimension bracket at the bottom is labelled 'Horizontal displacement = elapsed time (scaled by time-base in s/div)'. Annotations state 'The screen is a graph: vertical shows voltage, horizontal shows time'.
what_to_notice: The oscilloscope screen is not pre-printed with fixed voltage or time numbers. The graticule is a blank geometric grid whose axes are scaled by the external y-gain and time-base control settings.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Measuring signal amplitude with the y-gain: "A microphone detects sound waves and generates an alternating potential difference across the vertical input terminals."
purpose: Provide authentic examiner evidence of a sound wave displayed on a CRO screen, showing how 1.5 cycles span 6.0 cm on a calibrated graticule.
what_to_show: Authentic examination figure from Cambridge paper 9702/22/F/M/23 Question 5 Fig. 5.1 showing a square CRO graticule 6 major divisions wide by 6 major divisions high with fine grid lines (5 subdivisions per 1.0 cm). Dimension markers indicate 1.0 cm horizontal and 1.0 cm vertical major squares. A horizontal dashed centre line is located at y = 3.0 cm. A sinusoidal trace displays an amplitude of 1.0 cm (peaks at y = 4.0 cm, troughs at y = 2.0 cm), with exactly 1.5 cycles spanning the full 6.0 cm width.
what_to_notice: Notice that the waveform oscillates symmetrically about the central dashed equilibrium line. The amplitude is 1.0 cm (one major division from centre line to crest), not the 2.0 cm total peak-to-peak span.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Peak voltage versus peak-to-peak voltage: "The peak-to-peak voltage is exactly twice the signal amplitude."
purpose: Demonstrate the precise geometric extraction of signal amplitude and peak voltage from the equilibrium centre line, explicitly contrasting it with incorrect peak-to-peak measurement.
what_to_show: A two-panel comparative schematic on an oscilloscope graticule. Left panel: green vertical dimension arrow from the central dashed equilibrium line to the crest labelled 'Correct: Amplitude = Peak voltage V_0 = 2.5 div x 0.40 V div^-1 = 1.0 V'. Right panel: red vertical double-headed arrow spanning from trough to crest labelled 'Peak-to-peak voltage V_p-p = 5.0 div x 0.40 V div^-1 = 2.0 V' with a prominent warning note stating 'V_p-p is twice the amplitude. Divide by 2 to find signal amplitude'.
what_to_notice: Signal amplitude is strictly defined as maximum displacement from equilibrium. Measuring full peak-to-peak height without dividing by two is a major student error that doubles the true amplitude.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Measuring period and frequency with the time-base: "The horizontal separation between two successive identical points represents the time period of one complete cycle."
purpose: Provide authentic examiner evidence of an electromagnetic wave trace displayed on an oscilloscope, illustrating time-base measurement across 6.0 cm and wavelength calculation.
what_to_show: Authentic examination figure from Cambridge paper 9702/22/F/M/24 Question 5 Fig. 5.1 showing a rectangular CRO graticule 9 major divisions wide by 6 major divisions high with 1.0 cm square grid lines. A solid sinusoidal wave trace has its central crest at x = 5.0 cm and flanking troughs at x = 2.0 cm and x = 8.0 cm. The horizontal distance between successive troughs is exactly 6.0 cm, representing one complete wave cycle.
what_to_notice: One complete cycle can be measured between any two identical points in phase. Here, measuring between the two troughs from x = 2.0 cm to x = 8.0 cm directly gives the 6.0 cm cycle width for period calculation.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Measuring period and frequency with the time-base: "Measuring across several cycles spreads the reading uncertainty across the entire measured span."
purpose: Model multi-cycle measurement on a CRO trace to minimize fractional uncertainty in period determination, followed by the reciprocal conversion to frequency.
what_to_show: A CRO graticule displaying three full sinusoidal cycles across 12.0 horizontal divisions. A horizontal blue bracket spanning all three cycles is labelled 'Total span = 12.0 div; time-base = 25 micro-s div^-1'. An annotated step-by-step calculation shows: Step 1: Total time = 12.0 div x 25 micro-s div^-1 = 300 micro-s. Step 2: Period T = 300 micro-s / 3 cycles = 100 micro-s = 1.00 x 10^-4 s. Step 3: Frequency f = 1 / T = 1 / (1.00 x 10^-4 s) = 1.00 x 10^4 Hz = 10.0 kHz. Annotation highlights: 'Measuring N cycles reduces fractional uncertainty by factor N'.
what_to_notice: Measuring across 3 cycles spreads the reading uncertainty of +-0.1 division over 12 divisions instead of 4, reducing fractional uncertainty by a factor of 3 before taking the reciprocal to find frequency.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Deriving the wave equation: "During one period, the wave pattern advances forward by exactly one wavelength."
purpose: Demonstrate the geometric derivation of the wave equation v = f lambda by showing a progressive wave advancing by one wavelength during one period of particle oscillation.
what_to_show: Two vertically stacked time snapshots of a progressive transverse wave. Upper panel at t = 0 shows a sinusoidal waveform with crest 1 aligned with a vertical dashed reference line; a particle on the medium at x = 0 is marked with an orange circle at equilibrium. Lower panel at t = T shows the entire wave profile translated to the right by distance lambda, bringing crest 2 into alignment with the reference line. The orange particle has completed one full oscillation cycle (up, down, back to equilibrium) with zero net forward displacement. Accompanying text shows: 'Speed = distance / time = lambda / T = lambda / (1/f) = f lambda'.
what_to_notice: Notice that medium particles do not travel along with the wave; each particle merely oscillates in place. It is the advancing waveform that travels distance lambda in time T.

anchor: Measuring amplitude and frequency with a CRO and the wave equation > Deriving the wave equation for a wave train: "In a continuous wave train, each complete oscillation creates one additional wave cycle."
purpose: Provide authentic examiner evidence of a microphone trace displaying multiple cycles used to determine frequency and derive wave properties.
what_to_show: Authentic examination figure from Cambridge paper 9702/21/M/J/19 Question 5 Fig. 5.1 showing a rectangular CRO graticule 10 major divisions wide by 4 major divisions high with 1.0 cm grid lines. A sinusoidal wave trace displays three identical crests at x = 1.0 cm, 5.0 cm, and 9.0 cm, each reaching y = 3.5 cm (amplitude 1.5 cm above centre line at y = 2.0 cm). Two complete cycles span exactly 8.0 cm (4.0 cm per cycle). With time-base 0.20 ms cm^-1, T = 0.80 ms and f = 1250 Hz.
what_to_notice: Notice that two full cycles span from x = 1.0 cm to x = 9.0 cm, giving 8.0 cm for 2 cycles (4.0 cm per cycle). Using multiple cycles ensures maximum precision when extracting period.
